tool.name: Angular
tool.tagline: Batteries-included TypeScript framework with signals and standalone components
tool.description: Angular is a complete, opinionated framework from Google for building web applications in TypeScript, with routing, forms, HTTP, testing and server rendering built in. Modern Angular is built on standalone components, signals for fine-grained reactivity and a new template control flow, and runs zoneless by default. It is popular for large enterprise apps where consistency and long-term structure matter.

glossary.def: In Angular, one self-contained piece of the page, such as a header or a product card: a TypeScript class plus its HTML template and styles.
A modern Angular component that lists for itself, in its imports, everything its template uses, so no NgModule is needed.
The few optimised JavaScript and CSS files that a build produces from all your source files, ready for browsers to download.
In Angular, a component's HTML plus Angular's extra markup: {{ }} to show values, [ ] and ( ) bindings, and @if/@for blocks.
In Angular, a small box around a value that you read by calling it, like count(); when its value changes, everything that read it is told, so the page updates.
In an Angular template, a link between a spot in the page and a value or method in the component, which Angular keeps up to date.
Showing a value as text in an Angular template by writing it in double curly braces, like {{ name() }}.
Angular re-checking a component's template bindings and updating the page wherever a value has changed.
In Angular, a small formatter used in templates with the | symbol, like {{ price | currency }}, that turns a value into display text.
An Angular pipe that runs again only when its input or arguments change to a different value or object; the default kind.
In Angular, a class holding shared logic or data, created by Angular and handed to the components that ask for it with inject().
In Angular, an instruction telling dependency injection what to hand out when something asks for a service or setting.
The moments when Angular's inject() may be called: while Angular is creating a component, directive, pipe or service (constructor or field initializers), and in a few special functions.
The Angular object that creates service instances and hands them out; injectors form a tree that inject() searches upward.
An Angular class that adds behaviour to an existing element, like a component without its own template.
In Angular, the page element a component or directive is attached to, such as the <app-user-card> tag itself.
In Angular, a function that runs again whenever a signal it read changes, used for side effects such as saving to localStorage.
A method Angular calls at a set moment in a component's life, such as ngOnInit after the first inputs arrive or ngOnDestroy before removal.
Passing markup from a parent into a child component, which marks where it appears with <ng-content />.
An Angular function such as viewChild or contentChildren that finds elements or components in a template and returns them as a signal.
A name given to an element in an Angular template with #, like <input #search>, so other parts of the template or a query can refer to it.
An RxJS object representing a stream of values over time; nothing happens until you subscribe to it.
How well you can understand what a running system is doing from the outside, using its logs, metrics and traces.
A JavaScript library for working with streams of events and values (Observables), used by Angular's HttpClient, router and forms.
In RxJS, a function that takes a stream and returns a changed one, such as debounceTime (wait for a pause) or switchMap (switch to a new request).
An Angular function that sees every HttpClient request and response, used to add login headers, retry or handle errors in one place.
In Angular, an object that loads data asynchronously and exposes it as signals (value, isLoading, error), reloading when the signals it depends on change.
In Angular signal forms, the object form() returns: one field per property of your data, each giving its value and validation state as signals.
A function the Angular router runs before entering or leaving a route, which can allow, block or redirect the navigation.
In the Angular router, a function that loads data before a route opens and hands it to the page.
How TypeScript (or Node.js, or a bundler) works out which file or package an import refers to.
An attack where malicious input gets treated as code or commands, because the program glued untrusted text directly into them.
A separate JavaScript file the build splits off from the main bundle, downloaded only when that part of the app is needed.
Angular's testing helper that sets up a small Angular environment, with dependency injection and templates, for creating services and components in tests.
A library older Angular apps used to wrap the browser's event, timer and network functions so Angular could re-check the whole page after each one.
An Angular app running without zone.js: Angular updates the page only when notified, by a signal change, a template event or markForCheck.
An Angular change detection strategy (the default since v22) where a component is re-checked only when marked dirty: an input, event or signal it reads changed.
An Angular key, with a type, used to provide and inject values that aren't classes, such as configuration objects.
In Angular SSR, the browser-side step where Angular takes over the HTML the server sent, attaching events instead of rebuilding the page.

concepts.name: The Angular CLI and project structure
concepts.summary: Create, run and build an Angular app with the Angular CLI, and know what the generated files do.
concepts.why: The Angular CLI is how every Angular project is created, run, extended, tested and built.
concepts.body:
Angular is a **framework** for building web apps in TypeScript: a big ready-made structure where you fill in your parts and Angular decides when to run them. You build each page out of **components**, self-contained pieces such as a header, a product card or a login form, each with its own HTML, styles and TypeScript class.

You drive Angular through its **CLI** (command-line interface): a program called `ng` that you give commands to in the terminal. Install it once with `npm install -g @angular/cli`, then create a project with `ng new my-app`.

`ng serve` starts a **dev server**, a small web server on your own computer, at `http://localhost:4200`. Open that address in your browser and leave the server running while you work.

When you save a file, the page in the browser updates by itself (**hot reload**). To add a component, run `ng generate component user-card` (short: `ng g c user-card`); it creates the component's files. `ng generate` can also create other building blocks you'll meet later, such as services and pipes.

Two more commands: `ng test` runs the project's automated tests, and `ng build` produces the finished app in `dist/`. That output, a few optimised JavaScript and CSS files, is called the **bundle**. It's what you put on a real server for your users: the **production** version of the app.

A new project contains:
- `src/main.ts`: the starting point. It calls `bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig)` to start the app with its top-level component, `App`.
- `src/app/app.ts`, `app.html`, `app.css`: that top-level (root) component's class, HTML and styles.
- `src/app/app.config.ts`: app-wide settings, as a list of **providers** that switch on features such as page navigation (the router) and error reporting. The Services lesson explains providers.
- `src/app/app.routes.ts`: which URL shows which component (see the Routing lesson).
- `angular.json` holds build settings; `tsconfig.json` holds TypeScript settings, with strict checks on.

Older tutorials put components into groups called NgModules and name files `app.component.ts`. Modern Angular needs neither: each component lists for itself what it uses, which is why they're called **standalone** components.
takeaways: `ng new`, `ng serve`, `ng generate`, `ng test`, `ng build` cover the daily workflow
`main.ts` starts the root component with the providers from `app.config.ts`
New apps use standalone components; NgModules aren't needed
pitfalls: Following old tutorials that create NgModules and `app.component.ts` files; modern Angular doesn't need them.

quiz.q: Where do you register application-wide providers such as the router in a new Angular app?
options: In the providers array of app.config.ts passed to bootstrapApplication
quiz.explain: A new app passes an ApplicationConfig with its providers to bootstrapApplication in main.ts.

concepts.name: Components
concepts.summary: Define a component with @Component (selector, template, styles, imports) and use it inside another component.
concepts.why: Components are the building blocks of every Angular page.
concepts.body:
A component is a TypeScript class with an `@Component({...})` line just above it. That line is a **decorator**: a label, starting with `@`, that attaches extra information to a class. Here the information is a settings object telling Angular how to show the component on the page: - `selector`: the custom HTML tag that places the component, e.g. `'app-user-card'`, used as ``. Start selectors with a prefix such as `app-` so they never clash with real HTML elements. - `template` (written inline) or `templateUrl` (a separate `.html` file): the component's **template**, its HTML plus Angular's extra markup for showing data. - `styles` or `styleUrl`: CSS for this component only. Angular rewrites it so it matches only this component's elements; `p { color: red }` here won't touch paragraphs elsewhere. - `imports`: the other components (and other helpers you'll meet later) that this template uses. If you use `` without importing `Avatar`, the build fails with an "is not a known element" error. When Angular **renders** a component, it turns the template into real elements on the page and fills in the data. The data comes from the class: its **fields** (the properties declared in the class body) and methods are available to the template. Fields meant only for the template are usually marked `protected`: the template can see them, other code can't. Many fields hold **signals**, small boxes around a value that tell Angular when the value changes; you read one by calling it. The Signals lesson comes next. For now, `{{ ... }}` in a template means "show this value here": ```ts @Component({ selector: 'app-hello', template: `

Hello {{ name() }}

` }) export class Hello { protected name = signal('Ada'); } ``` Components form a tree: the root `App` component's template contains other components, whose templates contain more. Keep each one small and focused: a page component is built from smaller components that each do one job.
takeaways: `@Component` = selector + template + styles + imports on a TypeScript class
List every component (and other helper) the template uses in `imports`
A component's styles apply only to that component
pitfalls: Forgetting to add a child component to `imports`, causing "is not a known element" build errors.

quiz.q: A template uses <app-chart> but the build reports "'app-chart' is not a known element". What is the most likely fix?
options: Add the Chart component class to this component's imports array
quiz.explain: Standalone components must list every component their template uses in imports.

concepts.name: Signals: signal and computed
concepts.summary: Hold state in signals, update it with set and update, and derive values with computed.
concepts.why: Signals hold the changing data of a modern Angular app and tell Angular exactly which parts of the page to update.
concepts.body:
A **signal** is a small box around a value. When the value changes, the signal tells everything that uses it, including the templates that show it, so Angular can update just those parts of the page.

```ts
count = signal(0);        // WritableSignal<number>
count();                  // read: call it like a function
count.set(5);             // replace the value
count.update((c) => c + 1);   // compute from the previous value
```

Read a signal by calling it. Change it with `set(newValue)`, or with `update(fn)`, which works out the new value from the old one.

**`computed`** creates a read-only signal whose value is calculated from other signals:

```ts
double = computed(() => this.count() * 2);
```

Angular notes which signals a computed reads. It recalculates only when one of them has changed and someone reads the result; otherwise it hands back the value it remembered. If a branch of your function reads a signal only sometimes, the computed watches that signal only while the branch runs.

When a template reads a signal, Angular knows exactly which component to refresh when that signal changes. That's how modern Angular keeps the page up to date without re-checking everything. (In the example, `(click)="add()"` calls `add()` when the button is clicked; the Event binding lesson covers this.)

Rules that prevent bugs:
- **Don't change arrays or objects in place.** `this.items().push(x)` changes the array without telling anyone. Give the signal a new array instead: `items.update((list) => [...list, x])`.
- Setting a value equal to the current one (compared with `Object.is`) does nothing. An `equal` option lets you choose your own comparison.
- Keep computed functions free of side effects: they should only calculate, never set other signals.
- `asReadonly()` gives out a read-only view, so only the owner can write.
takeaways: Read a signal by calling it; write with `set` or `update`
`computed` recalculates only when a signal it read changes, and remembers its result
Replace arrays and objects instead of changing them in place
pitfalls: Changing an array or object inside a signal in place and expecting the page to update.

quiz.q: `items = signal([1, 2])`, then `items().push(3)`. A template shows items().length. What does it show?
options: 2, because the signal never learned about the change
quiz.explain: push changes the array in place without calling set or update, so the signal never tells anyone.

concepts.name: Template bindings
concepts.summary: Show data with interpolation and bind DOM properties, attributes, classes and styles with square brackets.
concepts.why: Bindings are how component data reaches the page; mixing up properties and attributes is a classic Angular bug.
concepts.body:
A template is HTML plus **bindings**: links between a spot in the page and a value in your component. Angular keeps every binding up to date as the component's data changes.

**Interpolation**, `{{ expression }}`, shows a value as text. Inside the braces you can use most simple TypeScript: property access, method calls, operators, template literals, `?.` and `??`. You can't assign, use `new` or write full statements.

Angular re-checks bindings whenever something may have changed; this re-checking is called **change detection**. It can happen often, so expressions in templates should be quick and have no side effects.

**Property binding** uses square brackets: `[disabled]="isSaving()"`, `[src]="avatarUrl()"`. It sets a property of the DOM element (or an input of a component, see Inputs and outputs) to the value, keeping its type: booleans stay booleans. Without brackets, `disabled="false"` sets the HTML attribute to the text "false", which still disables the button.

Some things exist only as HTML attributes, with no matching DOM property: ARIA attributes (extra labels for screen readers, like `aria-label`), `colspan`, attributes of SVG drawings, and `data-*`. Bind them with **`[attr.name]`**: `[attr.aria-label]="label()"`. A `null` value removes the attribute.

**Class and style bindings**:
- `[class.active]="isActive()"` turns one CSS class on or off; `[class]="{ active: a(), disabled: d() }"` takes an object, array or string.
- `[style.width.px]="width()"` sets one style with a unit; `[style]="{ color: c() }"` takes an object.

Angular also cleans (**sanitises**) values bound to `innerHTML`, URLs and styles, removing anything that could run a script, to block XSS attacks. And you can declare a variable inside a template with **`@let`**: `@let total = price() * qty();`.
takeaways: `{{ }}` renders text; `[prop]="expr"` binds DOM properties and inputs with real types
Use `[attr.x]` for attributes such as ARIA and colspan
`[class.x]`, `[style.prop.unit]` and object forms handle classes and styles
pitfalls: Writing `disabled="{{ isDisabled }}"` or `disabled="false"`; use `[disabled]="isDisabled()"`.

quiz.q: Which binding correctly sets an ARIA attribute from component state?
quiz.explain: aria-label is an attribute without a matching DOM property, so it needs the attr. prefix.

concepts.name: Event binding
concepts.summary: Respond to user actions with (event) bindings, read $event, and use key event filters.
concepts.why: Every interactive feature starts with an event handler.
concepts.body:
**Event binding** uses parentheses: `(click)="save()"`. When the event happens, Angular runs the code in the quotes, usually a call to a method on the component.

- Pass the browser's event object with **`$event`**: `(input)="onInput($event)"`. Give the parameter a type in the method and read the element from it: `(event.target as HTMLInputElement).value`.
- The code can be a short assignment or call: `(click)="count.set(count() + 1)"`. Put real logic in methods, so the template only says *what* happens.
- **Key filters**: `(keyup.enter)="send()"`, `(keydown.escape)="close()"`, or combinations like `(keydown.control.s)="save($event)"`.
- Any DOM event works, and a component's own events (outputs, a later lesson) use the same parentheses.
- Events on the whole window or document, like `(window:resize)`, go in the component's `host` setting: `host: { '(window:resize)': 'onResize()' }`.

Call `event.preventDefault()` in your handler to stop the browser's default action, such as following a link.

An event handler in a template tells Angular to run change detection, so even updating a plain field inside it refreshes the page. Changes made elsewhere, in a timer or after a promise, should go through signals, which notify Angular themselves. The simplest rule: keep all template data in signals.
takeaways: `(event)="handler($event)"` binds DOM events and component outputs
Key filters like `(keyup.enter)` avoid manual key checks
Keep the code in the quotes to a single method call
pitfalls: Forgetting to call the method: `(click)="save"` does nothing; write `(click)="save()"`.

quiz.q: What is $event in (input)="onInput($event)" on an <input>?
quiz.explain: For DOM events, $event is the browser's event object; read the value from its target.

concepts.name: Control flow: @if, @for, @switch
concepts.summary: Show or hide parts of a template and repeat elements with the built-in @if, @for (with track) and @switch blocks.
concepts.why: Every list and every condition in an Angular template uses these blocks, and track decides how fast lists update.
takeaways: `@if (cond; as x) {} @else {}`, `@switch` / `@case` / `@default`
`@for (x of list; track x.id) {} @empty {}`: track is mandatory
Use `$index`, `$first`, `$last` etc. via `let`
pitfalls: Tracking by `$index` (or by the object itself when the data is downloaded again) in lists that change, so every item's elements get rebuilt.

quiz.q: Why does @for require a track expression?
options: So Angular can recognise items across changes and reuse or move their elements
quiz.explain: Tracking by a stable id lets Angular match items between updates instead of destroying and recreating their elements.

concepts.name: Inputs and outputs
concepts.summary: Pass data into components with input() and send events out with output().
concepts.why: Inputs and outputs are a component's public face: how a parent sends data in and hears back from its children.
concepts.body:
Components receive data from their parent through **inputs** and tell the parent about events through **outputs**.

**Inputs** are declared with the `input()` function, which returns a read-only signal:

```ts
name = input.required<string>();     // parent must provide it
size = input(48);                    // optional with default
disabled = input(false, { transform: booleanAttribute });
```

The parent binds with brackets, `<app-avatar [name]="user().name" [size]="64" />`, or, for a string, as a plain attribute: `size="lg"`. Because inputs are signals, you can derive from them with `computed(() => this.size() * 2)`.

Required inputs can't be read before Angular sets them, so don't read them in the constructor. Read them in templates, in `computed`, or in methods Angular calls later (lifecycle hooks, a Practical lesson). A **transform** converts the incoming value: `booleanAttribute` turns a bare `<app-x disabled />` into `true`.

**Outputs** are declared with `output()`:

```ts
selected = output<User>();
this.selected.emit(user);
```

The parent listens with the same parentheses as DOM events: `(selected)="onSelect($event)"`, where `$event` is the emitted value. Unlike DOM events, outputs don't bubble up to elements further out.

Keep inputs read-only (the child never writes to them; `input()` signals have no `set`), and name outputs after what happened (`selected`, `closed`), not after what the parent should do. An `alias` option gives an input or output a different public name; use it sparingly. Older code uses `@Input()` and `@Output()` decorators with `EventEmitter`; they still work.
takeaways: `input()` / `input.required<T>()` declare inputs as read-only signals
`output<T>()` declares events; `emit(value)` sends them, parents get `$event`
Don't read required inputs in the constructor
pitfalls: Reading a required input in the constructor, which throws because it hasn't been set yet.

quiz.q: A child declares `closed = output<string>()` and calls this.closed.emit('esc'). How does the parent receive 'esc'?
quiz.explain: Outputs are bound with event syntax; $event holds the emitted value.

concepts.name: Services and dependency injection
concepts.summary: Put shared logic and state in services and get them anywhere with inject().
concepts.why: Services are how Angular apps share data and logic between components, talk to servers and stay easy to test.
concepts.body:
Components should focus on what the user sees. Logic that several components share, or that isn't about the page (talking to a server, keeping app-wide data, formatting), goes into a **service**: a plain class whose instance Angular creates and shares.

Instead of each component making its own copy with `new`, a component asks Angular for the service and Angular hands over the shared instance. This handing-out is called **dependency injection** (DI): what a component needs is given to it from outside rather than built by it.

In Angular 22 the CLI generates services with the **`@Service()`** decorator. It makes the class available everywhere in the app as a **singleton**, meaning exactly one shared instance:

```ts
@Service()
export class CartStore { ... }
```

Most existing code and libraries use the long-standing equivalent, `@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })`. With either, a service that nothing uses is left out of the bundle.

To use a service, call **`inject()`** in a field initializer (or the constructor):

```ts
export class CartBadge {
  private cart = inject(CartStore);
}
```

`inject()` works only in an **injection context**: while Angular is creating a component or service (or another of its building blocks), plus a few special functions you'll meet later. Calling it later, in a click handler for example, throws an error.

Why not just import one shared object from a module? With DI, Angular controls how long each instance lives and who shares it: one for the whole app, or one per component and everything inside it. Tests can also swap in a fake by giving Angular a different **provider**, the instruction that says what to hand out for a service. Constructor parameters (`constructor(private cart: CartStore)`) are the older way to inject and still work.

A service with signals makes a simple, effective **store** for app data: private writable signals, public read-only signals and computeds, and methods that update them.
takeaways: Services hold shared logic and state; components inject them
`@Service()` (v22) or `@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })` makes an app-wide singleton
Call `inject()` only in an injection context such as field initializers
pitfalls: Calling `inject()` inside an event handler or `setTimeout`, outside an injection context.

quiz.q: Two unrelated components both call inject(CartStore), which is provided in root. What do they get?
options: Copies that sync on change detection
quiz.explain: A root-provided service is created once and shared by everything in the app.

concepts.name: Pipes
concepts.summary: Format values in templates with built-in pipes like date, currency and json, and write a custom pure pipe.
concepts.why: Pipes keep formatting out of components and are reused across the whole app.
concepts.body:
A **pipe** transforms a value for display, right in the template: `{{ value | pipeName:arg1:arg2 }}`. You can chain pipes; they apply left to right.

Common built-in pipes come from `@angular/common`; add each one you use to the component's `imports`:
- `date`: `{{ createdAt | date:'mediumDate' }}` or a format like `'yyyy-MM-dd'`.
- `currency`, `number` (`'1.0-2'` = at least 1 digit before the point, 0 to 2 after it), `percent`.
- `uppercase`, `lowercase`, `titlecase`, `slice`, `keyvalue`.
- `json` shows an object as text, handy while developing.
- `async` shows the latest value of a Promise (or of an RxJS Observable, covered later) and keeps it updated.

Formatting follows the app's locale (`LOCALE_ID`), so dates and currencies appear the way users in that region expect.

A **custom pipe** is a class with `@Pipe({ name })` and a `transform(value, ...args)` method. Pipes are **pure** by default: Angular calls `transform` again only when the input value or an argument changes by reference, that is, becomes a different object. That makes them cheap, but it also means changing an array in place won't re-run a pure pipe. Impure pipes (`pure: false`) run on every change detection and should be avoided for anything slow.

For formatting, a pipe beats calling a method in the template, because a method runs again on every change detection. For data that only one component derives, a `computed` signal is usually clearer.
takeaways: `{{ value | pipe:arg }}` formats values; chain pipes left to right
Import pipes like `DatePipe` and `CurrencyPipe` into the component
Custom pipes are pure by default and only re-run when inputs change by reference
pitfalls: Changing an array in place and expecting a pure pipe that filters it to update.

quiz.q: A pure custom pipe filters an array. You push a new item into the same array. Does the displayed result change?
options: No, the array reference didn't change so the pure pipe isn't re-run
Only if the pipe is in imports
quiz.explain: Pure pipes re-run only when the input reference or arguments change.

concepts.name: effect, linkedSignal and untracked
concepts.summary: Run side effects when signals change, create writable state that resets from a source, and read signals without tracking.
concepts.why: Real apps must sync signals with storage, the console and code not written for Angular, and keep related state consistent.
takeaways: `effect` is for side effects outside signals; create it in an injection context
`linkedSignal` = writable state that resets when its source changes
`untracked` reads a signal without the effect or computed watching it
pitfalls: Using an effect to set one signal from another; that causes extra cycles and glitches. Use computed or linkedSignal.

quiz.q: A list of options can change, and the selection should reset to the first option when it does, while users can still pick another. What fits best?
quiz.explain: linkedSignal is writable like a signal but recomputes from its source whenever the source changes.

concepts.name: Two-way binding with model()
concepts.summary: Build components that support [(value)] two-way binding with model() signals.
concepts.why: Custom inputs, toggles and pickers should be as easy to bind as native form controls.
concepts.body:
**Two-way binding** combines a property binding and an event binding: `[(value)]="x"` is shorthand for `[value]="x" (valueChange)="x = $event"` (the "banana in a box" syntax).

The **`model()`** function creates both sides in one declaration:

```ts
checked = model(false);          // ModelSignal<boolean>
this.checked.set(true);          // updates locally AND emits checkedChange
```

A model is a writable signal inside the child. When the child calls `set` or `update`, Angular emits `checkedChange` and the parent's bound value updates. When the parent's value changes, the model receives it like an input.

In the parent, bind a **writable signal** directly: `<app-toggle [(checked)]="darkMode" />` where `darkMode = signal(false)`. Angular reads and writes the signal for you (note: no parentheses after `darkMode`). Binding a plain field also works.

`model.required<T>()` makes the binding mandatory. A model can also be used one-way: the parent can just pass `[checked]="x"` or just listen with `(checkedChange)`.

Use `model()` for value-like components (rating, toggle, date picker, tabs' active index). For components that should plug into Angular forms (checking the input against rules, tracking whether the user has visited the field), signal forms let custom controls implement a small interface built on `model()` too.
takeaways: `model()` declares a writable, two-way bindable signal input
Bind a writable signal directly: `[(value)]="score"` without calling it
pitfalls: Writing `[(value)]="score()"` with parentheses; two-way binding needs the signal itself, not its value.

quiz.q: Inside a child, `open = model(false)` and the code calls this.open.set(true). What happens?
options: Angular throws because models are read-only
The child's value changes and openChange is emitted so a two-way bound parent updates
quiz.explain: Setting a model signal updates it and emits the matching Change event.

concepts.name: Content projection and queries
concepts.summary: Pass markup into components with ng-content and reach child elements and components with viewChild and contentChild.
concepts.why: Layout components (cards, dialogs, tabs) depend on projection, and integrations need direct element access.
concepts.body:
**Content projection** lets a parent pass markup into a child. The child marks where it goes with ``: ```html

Any content

 ``` Several slots use `select` with a CSS selector: `` receives elements with that attribute, and a plain `` takes the rest. Fallback content can go inside `` itself. Projected content is created by the parent and belongs to it; the child can't decide when to create it or create it twice. When the child must control that (show it later, or repeat it), pass an `` instead and show it with `ngTemplateOutlet`. **View queries** and **content queries** give a component references to things in its template or its projected content, as signals: - `viewChild('ref')` finds an element or component marked `#ref` in its own template (a **template reference variable**); `viewChild(ChildComponent)` finds one by class. For a plain element you get an `ElementRef`, a wrapper whose `nativeElement` is the DOM element. - `viewChild.required(...)` when it always exists; `viewChildren(...)` for all matches. - `contentChild(...)` and `contentChildren(...)` search **projected** content, e.g. a tabs component finding its `` children. Query signals are `undefined` until Angular has created the view, so read them in `computed`, `effect`, event handlers or `afterNextRender` (which runs code once the page has been drawn), not in the constructor.
takeaways: `<ng-content />` projects parent markup; `select` creates named slots
`viewChild`/`viewChildren` search the component's own template
`contentChild`/`contentChildren` query projected content; results are signals
pitfalls: Reading a view query in the constructor, before the view exists.

quiz.q: A Tabs component needs the list of <app-tab> elements the parent placed between its tags. Which query fits?
quiz.explain: Projected content is queried with content queries; view queries only see the component's own template.

concepts.name: Lifecycle hooks, DestroyRef and render hooks
concepts.summary: Run code at the right moment: ngOnInit, ngOnChanges, ngOnDestroy, DestroyRef, afterNextRender and afterRenderEffect.
concepts.why: Initialising data, cleaning up subscriptions and touching the DOM safely all depend on lifecycle timing.
concepts.body:
Angular calls **lifecycle hooks** on components and directives as they are created, updated and destroyed. Implement them as methods (and add the matching interface, such as `OnInit`, so TypeScript checks the method name):
- `ngOnInit()`: once, after the first inputs are set. The classic place to start loading data based on inputs.
- `ngOnChanges(changes)`: whenever inputs declared the older way, with `@Input()`, change. With signal inputs you rarely need it: use `computed` or `effect`.
- `ngOnDestroy()`: before the component is removed; clean up timers and subscriptions to data streams.
- `ngAfterViewInit()` and `ngAfterContentInit()`: after the view or projected content is first created.

**`DestroyRef`** is a more flexible alternative to `ngOnDestroy`: `inject(DestroyRef).onDestroy(() => ...)` works in services, directives and helper functions, which is how helpers like `takeUntilDestroyed` clean up automatically.

For work on the page's elements, use the **render hooks**:
- `afterNextRender(fn)` runs once after Angular next updates the page, in the browser only. Use it to set up charts, measure elements or focus inputs.
- `afterRenderEffect(fn)` runs after each update whenever signals it reads change.
- `afterEveryRender(fn)` runs after every update (use sparingly).

Angular can also build pages on the server before sending them (server-side rendering, an Expert lesson). Render hooks never run there, so they are the safe place for browser-only features such as `window` or measuring elements. All of these registration functions must be called in an injection context, typically the constructor.
takeaways: `ngOnInit` after first inputs; `ngOnDestroy` or `DestroyRef.onDestroy` for cleanup
With signal inputs prefer `computed`/`effect` over `ngOnChanges`
`afterNextRender` / `afterRenderEffect` for browser-only DOM work
pitfalls: Touching `window` or the DOM in the constructor or ngOnInit of an SSR app; use render hooks.

quiz.q: Where should you initialise a third-party chart library that needs the canvas element, in an app that also renders on the server?
quiz.explain: afterNextRender runs after the DOM is rendered and only in the browser.

concepts.name: Routing
concepts.summary: Configure routes, show them with router-outlet, link with routerLink, load page code on demand and read URL parameters as inputs.
concepts.why: Every multi-page Angular app is built around the router.
concepts.body:
The Angular **router** decides which component to show for the current URL, so one app can have many pages without the browser reloading. Define a `Routes` array and register it with `provideRouter(routes)` in `app.config.ts`:

```ts
export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', component: Home, title: 'Home' },
  { path: 'products/:id', loadComponent: () => import('./product/product').then((m) => m.ProductPage) },
  { path: '**', component: NotFound },
];
```

- The root template contains `<router-outlet />` (import `RouterOutlet`): that's where the matched component appears.
- **Lazy loading** with `loadComponent` (one component) or `loadChildren` (a list of child routes) puts that page's code in a separate file that the browser downloads only when the user first visits the page, keeping the first download small.
- `children` define nested routes, shown in a nested outlet; `redirectTo` with `pathMatch: 'full'` sends the user on to another path; `'**'` catches every other URL (put it last, because routes match in order).
- `title` sets the browser tab's title.

**Navigation**: `<a routerLink="/products/42">` or `[routerLink]="['/products', p.id]"` (import `RouterLink`), with `routerLinkActive="active"` to style the current link. In code, `inject(Router).navigate(['/products', id])`.

**Reading parameters**: with `provideRouter(routes, withComponentInputBinding())`, the `:id` parts of the path, the query string parameters and resolved data are bound to component inputs of the same name: `id = input.required<string>()`. Because it is a signal, the component updates when you navigate from `/products/1` to `/products/2` (the same component instance is reused). Without input binding, inject `ActivatedRoute` and subscribe to its Observables (RxJS streams, covered with HttpClient).
takeaways: Define `Routes`, `provideRouter(routes)`, show pages in `<router-outlet />`
Lazy-load page code with `loadComponent` / `loadChildren`
`withComponentInputBinding()` maps URL parameters to inputs; the component is reused when only parameters change
pitfalls: Placing the `'**'` catch-all route before other routes; matching is first-come, so it swallows everything.

quiz.q: Navigating from /products/1 to /products/2 shows the same component. With withComponentInputBinding and id = input.required<string>(), what happens?
options: The same instance is reused and the id() signal changes to '2'
The component is destroyed and recreated
quiz.explain: The router reuses the component when only params change; signal inputs make the change visible.

concepts.name: HttpClient and interceptors
concepts.summary: Call web APIs with HttpClient, type responses, handle errors and add behaviour to every request with functional interceptors.
concepts.why: Talking to a server is central to most Angular apps, and interceptors keep login headers and error handling in one place.
concepts.body:
**`HttpClient`** (from `@angular/common/http`) is Angular's way to send HTTP requests to a web API. It is available for injection by default and uses `fetch` under the hood. You switch on extra features with `provideHttpClient(...)` in `app.config.ts`.

```ts
private http = inject(HttpClient);
getUsers() { return this.http.get<User[]>('/api/users'); }
```

Its methods (`get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`) return an **Observable**, from **RxJS**, a library for streams of values over time that Angular uses. An Observable is like a newsletter: nothing arrives until you subscribe, and each subscriber gets its own delivery.

- Observables from HttpClient are **cold**: no request is sent until something subscribes (`.subscribe()`, the `async` pipe, `toSignal`, `firstValueFrom`). Each subscription sends a new request.
- The response body is read as JSON by default. The `<User[]>` part only tells TypeScript what to expect; nothing checks the real data while the app runs.
- Options include `params`, `headers`, `responseType`, and `observe: 'response'` to get the status and headers too.
- Errors arrive as an `HttpErrorResponse`, in the error callback or the RxJS `catchError` operator.

For most read-only data in components, prefer `httpResource` (next lesson), which wraps HttpClient in signals.

An **interceptor** is a function that sees every request and response:

```ts
export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) =>
  next(req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${inject(Auth).token()}` } }));
```

Register interceptors with `provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor]))`. Requests can't be changed in place, so make an altered copy with `clone`. Interceptors typically add login headers, write to the console, retry failed requests, show error messages and drive loading indicators.
takeaways: `inject(HttpClient).get<T>(url)` returns a cold Observable; nothing is sent until subscribed
The `<T>` type only informs TypeScript; nothing checks the data at runtime
Functional interceptors (`HttpInterceptorFn`) copy and modify every request
pitfalls: Calling `this.http.post(...)` without subscribing, so the request is never sent.

quiz.q: A service method returns this.http.delete('/api/items/1'), and a click handler calls it without subscribe(). What happens?
options: No request is sent because the Observable is never subscribed
quiz.explain: HttpClient observables are cold; the request is made per subscription.

concepts.name: Async data with resource and httpResource
concepts.summary: Load async data as signals with httpResource and resource: reactive params, loading and error state, reload and abort.
concepts.why: Resources are the signal-native way to fetch data in Angular, replacing hand-written loading and error flags.
concepts.body:
A **resource** turns asynchronous data into signals. It re-fetches automatically when the signals it depends on change, and it exposes state you can use in templates.

**`httpResource`** (from `@angular/common/http`) wraps HttpClient. Pass a function that returns the URL (or a request object); signals read inside it make the resource reactive:

```ts
user = httpResource<User>(() => `/api/users/${this.userId()}`);
```

**`resource`** (from `@angular/core`) works with any Promise-based loader:

```ts
weather = resource({
  params: () => ({ city: this.city() }),
  loader: ({ params, abortSignal }) => fetch(`/api/weather?city=${params.city}`, { signal: abortSignal }).then((r) => r.json()),
});
```

A resource exposes:

- `value()` — the data (`undefined` until loaded); `hasValue()` narrows it safely.
- `isLoading()`, `error()`, and `status()` (`'idle' | 'loading' | 'reloading' | 'resolved' | 'error' | 'local'`).
- `reload()` to fetch again, and `set`/`update` to change the value locally, for example to show a change before the server has confirmed it.

When params change while a request is still running, the previous request is **aborted** (through `abortSignal`), so stale responses never win. If the params or URL function returns `undefined`, the loader doesn't run and the resource stays idle, a neat way to wait for required input.

Use resources for reading data. Requests that change data on the server (`POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) should be explicit calls in event handlers or form submission, followed by `reload()` if needed.
takeaways: `httpResource(() => url)` and `resource({ params, loader })` expose async data as signals
Use `value()`, `hasValue()`, `isLoading()`, `error()`, `status()` and `reload()`
Changing params aborts the in-flight request; returning undefined keeps it idle
pitfalls: Using a resource to send POST or DELETE requests; resources are for reading data.

quiz.q: The URL function of an httpResource returns undefined because no user is selected yet. What happens?
options: The resource stays idle and makes no request
It retries until a value appears
quiz.explain: Returning undefined from the request/params function means there is nothing to load yet.

concepts.name: Signal forms
concepts.summary: Build typed forms with checked input from a signal model with form(), schema rules and the [formField] directive.
concepts.why: Signal forms are Angular's newest way to build forms: less repetitive code than reactive forms, and built entirely on signals.
takeaways: `form(modelSignal, schemaFn)` builds a typed field tree that writes into the model
Bind inputs with `[formField]`; read state via `field().valid()`, `errors()`, `touched()`
Rules (`required`, `email`, `minLength`, `validate`...) are declared in the schema
`submit()` validates, tracks submitting and applies server errors
pitfalls: Keeping a separate copy of the data and syncing it with the form; the model signal already is the form value.

quiz.q: With signal forms, where is the current value of the whole form?
options: Only in loginForm.value property after submit
In the model signal passed to form(); the UI writes into it
quiz.explain: Signal forms use your writable signal as the source of truth, so model() always reflects user input.

concepts.name: RxJS and signals interop
concepts.summary: Convert between Observables and signals with toSignal, toObservable, takeUntilDestroyed, rxResource and outputFromObservable.
concepts.why: Much Angular code and many libraries are RxJS-based; mixing them cleanly with signals is an everyday senior skill.
concepts.body:
Signals hold a **current value**; RxJS Observables model **streams of events over time**, with **RxJS operators**, functions that reshape a stream: `debounceTime` waits for a pause, `switchMap` swaps to a new request, `retry` tries again. Angular's `@angular/core/rxjs-interop` package converts between the two.

- **`toSignal(obs$, { initialValue })`** subscribes immediately and exposes the latest value as a signal; it unsubscribes when the component or service is destroyed. Without `initialValue` the signal is `undefined` until the first value arrives; `{ requireSync: true }` is for sources like `BehaviorSubject` that already hold a value when you subscribe.
- **`toObservable(sig)`** turns a signal into an Observable that emits (a moment later, through an effect) when the signal changes, so you can apply operators like `debounceTime` and `switchMap`.
- **`takeUntilDestroyed()`** ends a subscription when the current component or service is destroyed. Call it in an injection context, or pass a `DestroyRef`.
- **`rxResource({ params, stream })`** works like `resource` (see the resources lesson) but loads from an Observable.
- **`outputFromObservable(obs$)`** exposes an Observable as a component output, and `outputToObservable` converts the other way.

A typical search-as-you-type setup: a signal holds the search text; `toObservable` plus `debounceTime`, `distinctUntilChanged` and `switchMap` turn it into server requests (cancelling outdated ones); then `toSignal` hands the results to the template.

Rule of thumb: use signals for state shown in templates, RxJS for coordinating complicated flows of events, and convert where the two meet.
takeaways: `toSignal` reads an Observable as a signal and unsubscribes automatically
`toObservable` lets you apply RxJS operators to signal changes
`takeUntilDestroyed()` ties subscriptions to the component lifetime
pitfalls: Calling `toSignal` inside a method or event handler, creating a new subscription each time (and failing outside an injection context).

quiz.q: Why use switchMap rather than mergeMap for a search-as-you-type request?
options: switchMap cancels the previous inner request when a new query arrives, so stale results can't overwrite new ones
quiz.explain: switchMap unsubscribes from the previous inner Observable, cancelling the outdated HTTP request.

concepts.name: Reactive forms
concepts.summary: Work with the established FormGroup/FormControl forms: typed forms, validators, formControlName and valueChanges.
concepts.why: Most existing Angular codebases and many libraries use reactive forms, so you need to read and maintain them.
concepts.body:
Before signal forms, the standard for complex forms was **reactive forms** (`ReactiveFormsModule`). They remain fully supported and are everywhere in existing code.

The form model is a tree of control objects created in the class:

- `FormControl` holds one value plus validation state.
- `FormGroup` groups named controls; `FormArray` holds a dynamic list.
- `FormBuilder` (via `inject(FormBuilder).nonNullable`) shortens creation: `fb.group({ email: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.email]] })`.

Forms are **strictly typed** since Angular 14: `form.value.email` is `string | undefined` (disabled controls are excluded from `value`), while `form.getRawValue()` includes everything. `nonNullable` makes `reset()` return to the initial value instead of `null`.

The template binds with directives: `[formGroup]="form"` on the `<form>`, `formControlName="email"` on inputs, `formGroupName`/`formArrayName` for nesting, and `(ngSubmit)` for submission.

Validation, checking input against rules: built-in `Validators` (`required`, `email`, `minLength`, `pattern`...), custom `ValidatorFn`s returning an error object or `null`, async validators, and group-level validators for cross-field rules. Check `control.hasError('required')`, `invalid`, `touched` and `dirty`.

Changes are exposed as Observables (RxJS streams of values): `valueChanges` and `statusChanges`, often combined with RxJS or converted with `toSignal`. Custom inputs integrate by implementing `ControlValueAccessor`.
takeaways: `FormGroup`/`FormControl`/`FormArray` model the form in the class; templates bind with `formControlName`
Forms are typed; `nonNullable` makes reset restore initial values
`valueChanges`/`statusChanges` are Observables; validators return error objects or null
pitfalls: Reading `form.value` and missing disabled controls; use `getRawValue()` when you need every value.

quiz.q: A control is disabled. Is its value included in form.value?
options: No, disabled controls are excluded from value; getRawValue() includes them
quiz.explain: FormGroup.value omits disabled controls, which is also reflected in its type.

concepts.name: Attribute directives and host bindings
concepts.summary: Add reusable behaviour to elements with attribute directives, host bindings and listeners, and compose them with hostDirectives.
concepts.why: Directives package shared behaviour (tooltips, permissions, autofocus) without wrapper components.
concepts.body:
A **directive** is like a component without a template: it attaches behaviour to an existing element. **Attribute directives** are selected by an attribute, e.g. `selector: '[appHighlight]'`, and applied with `

`. Inside a directive you can: - Accept inputs with `input()`. Using the selector's name as an input alias lets you write `

`. - Inject the **host element**, the element the directive sits on, with `inject(ElementRef)` (use sparingly; prefer bindings). - Declare **host bindings and listeners** (bindings and event listeners on the host element) in the `host` setting: `host: { '[class.active]': 'active()', '(mouseenter)': 'show()', 'role': 'button' }`. This is the recommended replacement for the `@HostBinding` and `@HostListener` decorators. - Inject services and other directives on the same element. Components can also use `host` to style or annotate their own host element. **`hostDirectives`** composes directives into a component or directive: `hostDirectives: [{ directive: Tooltip, inputs: ['tooltip'] }]` applies `Tooltip` to every instance and exposes its input, letting you build components from reusable behaviours without inheritance. **Structural directives** (with `*`, like the legacy `*ngIf`) create and remove pieces of the page from an ``; with built-in control flow you rarely need to write one. Remember to add directives to the `imports` of the components that use them.
takeaways: Attribute directives add behaviour via a selector like `[appX]`
Use `host: {...}` for host bindings and listeners instead of decorators
`hostDirectives` composes reusable behaviour into components
pitfalls: Changing the DOM directly through ElementRef when a host binding would do; it breaks server rendering and skips Angular's sanitising.

quiz.q:
How do you let `

` pass 'red' into a directive's color input?
quiz.explain: Aliasing an input to the selector name lets the attribute itself carry the value.

concepts.name: Route guards, resolvers and redirects
concepts.summary: Protect routes with functional guards (canActivate, canMatch, canDeactivate) and load data before a page opens with resolvers.
concepts.why: Login checks, permissions, unsaved-change warnings and data preloading are built on these router hooks.
concepts.body:
The router can run functions before it opens a route. A **guard** decides whether navigation may go ahead; modern guards are plain functions that can `inject()` services.

- **`canActivate`**: may the user enter this route? Return `true`, `false`, a `UrlTree` (to send the user elsewhere, e.g. `inject(Router).createUrlTree(['/login'])`), or a `RedirectCommand`; Promises and Observables that deliver these work too.
- **`canMatch`**: should this route definition even be considered? If false, the router tries the next matching route, and lazy-loaded code isn't downloaded. Good for showing different pages at the same path depending on the user's role (admin vs user dashboard).
- **`canActivateChild`**: guard every child route.
- **`canDeactivate`**: may the user leave? Receives the component instance, used for "unsaved changes" confirms.

Route **resolvers** (`ResolveFn<T>`) fetch data before the route activates; the result is available as route data, and with component input binding as an input of the same name. Resolvers delay navigation until data arrives, so use them for small, essential data; for most pages, loading in the component with a resource gives faster perceived navigation.

Guards only shape what the user sees: **always check permissions on the server too**, because anyone can skip your browser code and call the server directly.

Keep guards small and reusable, e.g. a `roleGuard('admin')` factory that returns a `CanActivateFn`.
takeaways: Guards are functions returning boolean, UrlTree/RedirectCommand, or async versions
`canMatch` also prevents lazy code from loading; `canDeactivate` guards leaving
Route resolvers preload data but delay navigation
Guards shape the user experience; enforce security on the server
pitfalls: Treating route guards as security; anyone can call your server's web API directly.

quiz.q: Which guard prevents a lazy-loaded admin bundle from even being downloaded for non-admins?
quiz.explain: If canMatch returns false the route isn't matched, so its loadChildren never runs.

concepts.name: Deferrable views with @defer
concepts.summary: Lazy-load parts of a template with @defer, triggers like on viewport and on interaction, prefetching and placeholder blocks.
concepts.why: @defer shrinks the first download and gets the page on screen sooner, with almost no code.
takeaways: `@defer (trigger) {}` splits used components into a lazy chunk
Triggers: idle (default), viewport, interaction, hover, immediate, timer, when
`prefetch on ...` downloads early; `@placeholder`, `@loading`, `@error` handle states
pitfalls: Importing a deferred component somewhere else in the same file (or using it outside the block), which makes it load up front.

quiz.q: A component is used inside @defer but also referenced in a ViewChild query in the same file. What happens?
options: It goes into the main bundle, so it is not deferred
quiz.explain: Dependencies are only deferred if they aren't referenced outside the @defer block in that file.

concepts.name: Testing components and services
concepts.summary: Test Angular code with TestBed and Vitest: set up providers, create components, wait for updates and fake HTTP.
concepts.why: Tests keep large Angular apps maintainable; TestBed lets you test with real dependency injection and templates.
concepts.body:
A **unit test** is a small automated test that checks one piece of code, such as a service or a component. New Angular projects run them with **Vitest** (older ones use Karma and Jasmine; the Angular tools below are the same). Run tests with `ng test`.

**TestBed** sets up a small Angular environment for a test, with dependency injection and template compiling:
- Services: `TestBed.inject(MyService)` after `TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [...] })`. Replace what a service needs with fakes (**mocks**) using `{ provide: Real, useValue: fake }`.
- Components: `const fixture = TestBed.createComponent(MyComponent)`; `fixture.componentInstance` is the class instance, `fixture.nativeElement` its DOM element.
- Set inputs with `fixture.componentRef.setInput('name', 'Ada')`.
- Angular updates the page a moment after state changes, not instantly, so **`await fixture.whenStable()`** after changing state or triggering events; `fixture.detectChanges()` forces an update immediately.

For HTTP, provide `provideHttpClient()` and `provideHttpClientTesting()`, then use **`HttpTestingController`**: `httpMock.expectOne('/api/todos').flush([...])` answers the request with fake data, and `httpMock.verify()` checks there were no unexpected requests.

Test behaviour as a user sees it: find elements in the page, click buttons (`button.click()`), check the text shown. **Component harnesses** (from Angular's Component Dev Kit) give a stable way to drive complex components such as Angular Material's.

Pure logic (pipes, utility functions, services built from computed signals) can be tested as plain classes without TestBed. For tests that drive a real browser through the whole app (end-to-end tests), use Playwright or Cypress.
takeaways: `TestBed.configureTestingModule` + `createComponent`/`inject` for tests with real DI
Use `setInput` for inputs and `await fixture.whenStable()` before checking the page
`provideHttpClientTesting` + `HttpTestingController` fake HTTP responses
pitfalls: Asserting on the DOM right after changing state without awaiting `whenStable()` or calling `detectChanges()`.

quiz.q: How do you set a signal input named 'user' on a component under test?
quiz.explain: Signal inputs are read-only from the class side; setInput sets them as a parent binding would.

concepts.name: Change detection: zoneless and OnPush
concepts.summary: Understand how Angular decides what to update: signals, OnPush (now the default), zoneless scheduling and markForCheck.
concepts.why: Change detection is the source of most Angular performance problems and the 'view didn't update' class of bugs.
concepts.body:
**Change detection** is how Angular brings the page in line with component state: it walks through the components' views, re-evaluates their template bindings, and updates the DOM where values changed.

Historically, **zone.js** wrapped the browser's own functions for events, timers and network requests, and checked the whole app after every one of them. Since Angular 21, new apps are **zoneless**: nothing is wrapped, and Angular schedules change detection only when it is **notified**. Notifications come from:

- a signal read in a template changing,
- a template or host-element event listener firing,
- `markForCheck()` (also called by the `async` pipe), `setInput`, or attaching a view.

Angular 22 also makes **`OnPush`** the default strategy (the old behaviour is now called `ChangeDetectionStrategy.Eager`). An OnPush component is checked only when it is **marked dirty**, flagged as needing a check because its inputs changed (by reference), an event fired in it, or a signal it reads changed. Signals go further: a signal change marks only the consuming component for refresh, so Angular can skip clean ancestors.

Consequences:

- Changing a plain field from a `setTimeout`, a promise or another library's callback won't update the view. Use signals (or call `markForCheck`).
- Mutating an input object in place doesn't change its reference, so OnPush children won't refresh.
- In development, Angular runs a second check and throws **NG0100 ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenChecked** if a binding changed during the check, which points to state updates in the wrong place.

Migrating older apps: `provideZonelessChangeDetection()` and components set to `Eager` ease the transition.
takeaways: Zoneless Angular renders only when notified: signals, template events, markForCheck
OnPush is the default in v22; components refresh when marked dirty
Prefer signals for all template state; mutate inputs immutably
NG0100 in dev reveals state changed during a check
pitfalls: Updating plain fields in timers or library callbacks and wondering why the zoneless view doesn't refresh.

quiz.q: In a zoneless app, a promise callback sets this.title = 'x' (a plain field) and nothing else happens. Does the view update?
options: Not necessarily; nothing notified Angular, so use a signal or markForCheck
quiz.explain: Without zone.js, Angular needs a notification such as a signal change to schedule rendering.

quiz.q: A parent mutates an object passed as an input to an OnPush child (obj.name = 'B'). Why might the child not update?
options: The input reference didn't change, so the child isn't marked dirty
quiz.explain: OnPush compares input references; in-place mutation keeps the same reference.

concepts.name: Hierarchical injectors and providers
concepts.summary: Master the injector tree: environment vs element injectors, provider types, InjectionToken, multi providers and lookup modifiers.
concepts.why: Scoping services correctly avoids bugs from accidentally shared data, enables per-feature configuration and powers library design.
concepts.body:
An **injector** is the object that creates and hands out service instances. Angular has a **tree of injectors**, and `inject(Token)` walks it from the requesting point upward until a provider is found.

- **Element injectors** come from `providers` (and `viewProviders`) in `@Component`/`@Directive`. Each component instance gets its own instance of those services, shared with its descendants. Use it for state scoped to a widget, e.g. one `FormState` per wizard.
- **Environment injectors** come from `bootstrapApplication` providers (root), `@Service()`/`providedIn: 'root'`, and route-level `providers`, which create a child environment injector for that route subtree (useful for feature-scoped configuration).

Resolution checks the element injector chain first (from the requesting element up to the root component), then the environment injector chain. If nothing is found, it throws `NullInjectorError`.

**Provider forms**: `{ provide: T, useClass: Impl }`, `useValue`, `useFactory: () => ...` (factories can call `inject`), and `useExisting` (alias). **`InjectionToken<T>`** provides non-class values (config objects, functions) with a type; it can carry its own `factory` to be tree-shakable. **`multi: true`** collects several providers into an array, so many parts of an app can each add an item; `HTTP_INTERCEPTORS` and form validators work this way.

Lookup modifiers, `inject(T, { optional, self, skipSelf, host })`, control the search: `optional` returns `null` instead of throwing; `self` looks only at the current element; `skipSelf` starts at the parent (useful for nested tree components); `host` stops at the host component.
takeaways: Element injectors (component providers) scope instances per component subtree
Environment injectors: root, application and route-level providers
useClass/useValue/useFactory/useExisting, InjectionToken and multi providers
`inject(T, { optional, self, skipSelf, host })` controls the lookup
pitfalls: Listing a service that holds data in a component's providers by accident, creating separate instances where one shared instance was expected.

quiz.q: Two sibling <app-counter-panel> components each list Counter in their providers. How many Counter instances exist?
options: It throws a duplicate provider error
quiz.explain: Element-level providers create an instance per component, shared only with that component's descendants.

concepts.name: SSR, hydration and render modes
concepts.summary: Build Angular pages on the server, choose a render mode per route, hydrate with event replay and incremental hydration, and avoid SSR bugs.
concepts.why: Server rendering puts content on screen sooner and lets search engines read it, but brings bugs that only happen on one side.
concepts.body:
With **server-side rendering** (SSR), the server runs your Angular app and sends finished HTML, so the page shows before the JavaScript arrives. Angular's SSR support lives in `@angular/ssr`. Create an app with `ng new --ssr` or add it with `ng add @angular/ssr`.

**Render modes per route** are configured in `app.routes.server.ts` with `ServerRoute` entries: `RenderMode.Prerender` (static HTML at build time, with `getPrerenderParams` for dynamic segments), `RenderMode.Server` (rendered per request) or `RenderMode.Client` (browser only). They are registered with `provideServerRendering(withRoutes(serverRoutes))` in the server config.

**Hydration** is the browser-side step that follows: Angular takes over the server-rendered DOM instead of re-creating it. It is enabled with `provideClientHydration()`; add `withEventReplay()` to record clicks that happen before the code loads and replay them, and `withIncrementalHydration()` to keep parts of the page dehydrated until needed: `@defer (hydrate on viewport)` or `hydrate on interaction` renders the content on the server but only downloads and hydrates its code when triggered.

HttpClient requests made during SSR are saved into the HTML and reused in the browser (the HTTP transfer cache), so data isn't fetched twice.

Pitfalls:

- No `window`, `document` layout or `localStorage` on the server. Use `afterNextRender` or check `isPlatformBrowser(inject(PLATFORM_ID))`, and inject `DOCUMENT` instead of the global.
- Hydration requires the DOM to match: direct DOM manipulation or invalid HTML nesting causes errors (`ngSkipHydration` is an escape hatch).
- Long-running timers or never-completing work keep the server waiting for the app to become stable.
- Server-side, services are per request, but module-level variables are shared between users.
takeaways: Per-route `RenderMode`: Prerender, Server or Client
`provideClientHydration()` with event replay and incremental hydration (`@defer (hydrate on ...)`)
Browser-only code goes in `afterNextRender` or behind `isPlatformBrowser`
HttpClient responses are transferred from server to client automatically
pitfalls: Reading `localStorage` during rendering, which crashes on the server or causes a hydration mismatch.

Renders it on the server, then downloads and hydrates its code when it enters the viewport
